You face two doors guarded by two guards. One always tells the truth, the other always lies, but you don't know which is which. One door leads to freedom, the other to disaster. You may ask exactly ONE question to exactly ONE guard. What question guarantees you find the door to freedom?
choices: Ask either guard: 'If I asked the other guard whether this door leads to freedom, what would they say?' — then pick the opposite door from their answer
Ask both guards the same question and see if they agree
Ask either guard: 'Are you the truth-teller?' — then trust whichever door they point to
Ask either guard: 'Does this door lead to freedom?' and believe whatever they say

You are shown two identical envelopes and told one contains exactly twice as much money as the other. You pick one at random and open it to find $100. You're offered the chance to switch. A tempting argument says: the other envelope holds either $50 or $200, each equally likely, so switching has an expected value of $125 — a gain over your $100. Is this switching argument correct?
choices: Yes, but only if you have no idea how much money might be in either envelope
No — the calculation invalidly treats $100 as fixed while the other side varies inconsistently; there is no rational reason to switch
Yes — you should always switch, since $125 expected value beats $100 for certain
No — you should never switch, because the first envelope you pick is always the larger one

questions.q: If it takes 6 people 6 days to dig 6 holes, how many days does it take 3 people to dig 3 holes?

An online retailer highlights that 95% of its published reviews are five stars and concludes nearly all customers love the product. Only customers who create an account and choose to write a review are counted. Is that 95% figure a reliable estimate of overall customer satisfaction?
choices: No — reviewers are a self-selected sample, so this isn't representative of all customers
No — five-star reviews are always fake and should be discounted entirely
Yes, as long as the review count is large enough, self-selection stops mattering
Yes — 95% is such a large majority that it must reflect true satisfaction
